title: Right Effort on the Eightfold Path
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: The talk's main teaching is that Right Effort in Soto Zen involves being aware of and working with our thoughts, feelings, and impulses to cultivate a more mindful and compassionate approach to life. This requires paying attention to negative influences and recognizing when we're stuck in unskillful states of mind, such as prejudice or frustration. By shifting our focus towards the beauty in the world, practicing gratitude, and acknowledging difficulties head-on, we can develop greater self-awareness and abandon patterns that lead to suffering, ultimately cultivating a more skillful and peaceful way of being.

The eight steps of the path are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, the one I'm talking about tonight, right effort, and then right mindfulness and right concentration.

Right effort is about working with what arises in the mind, being aware of thoughts, feelings, impulses to say or do something, and then making conscious decisions about what to say and do.
In the course of our lives, people are always growing and developing and learning things.
Early in life, we learn how to walk, we learn how to speak, we learn how to read, we learn how to socialize.
As you get older and become an adult, you learn how to be independent.
You learn how to work, further improving your social skills, hopefully.
People are growing and developing their entire lives, and generally speaking, people become better functioning as the years go by.
But all of us are also exposed to negative influences throughout our life, unhealthy influences.

This could be through social media, advertising, opinions of family members and friends, some negative values that are embedded in our culture, racism, sexism, any form of discrimination or belief that may increase suffering for others.

That means, of the many things that arise in your mind, what will you engage with and what are you going to just let go of, be aware of and let go?

I think that's just a wonderful question.

How do you think he might have answered that question?
And then I'll tell you what he said.
He responded with four recommendations.
Number one, he said, avoid unskillful states of mind.
Number two, when you experience unskillful states of mind, abandon them.
Cultivate skillful, healthy states of mind.
And the fourth, maintain them.
Now that is such uncomplicated, straightforward piece of advice, very easy to understand.
Imagine if we could all do that.
Imagine if we could all avoid unhealthful states of mind and abandon them as soon as we recognize that one of them has arisen.
But it is not an easy thing to carry out because it requires paying attention.
As soon as you stop paying attention, then you have much less chance of being selective about what kinds of thoughts and feelings you act on or speak about.
In one of the talks I listened to, they gave the example of you can use driving on a multi-lane freeway as an example of the Buddha's advice.
If you're driving along in a lane and you're moving along fine, you just stay there.
If you see debris on the road or maybe there's an accident up ahead and cars are starting to back up, you would change lanes if you can.
So you avoid the lanes that have problems, that have traffic jam or debris, and you stay in the lanes where things are moving ahead if you can.
Now, I've found it pretty easy to pull out of negative thinking once I am aware of it.
The key is to be aware of it.

Sometimes I might be walking downtown and I'll just up comes some political thing I might have read in that morning's paper or heard the night before, and then pretty soon I'm chewing on it because there's a lot of political things going on that I don't like.

Then I might think, "Oh, you know, I don't really like the weather today," and then maybe it's all I got to do something this afternoon I don't want to do, and I can pretty soon I've got a little run of negative thoughts going.
Once I catch that, what I'll often do is I'll look at the sky.
In Bellingham in Washington, usually there's clouds, and they're really often quite beautiful, you know, the light, the shape.

Anyway, when I see something beautiful, whether it's clouds or maybe I hear a bird sing or a child laugh, that gets me out of my stream of negative thinking.
The joy and the beauty in the world is always here.
It's always around somewhere, no matter what kind of a day I'm having, no matter what kind of difficulties might be happening, happening in my personal life.
So I recommend that you keep an eye out for it.

Not some phony thing, not some cover up, but something I genuinely appreciate.
I can come up with a dozen things.
I'm grateful for this practice that I've had for so many years, I'm grateful for my wife and my daughter.
I love living in Bellingham, I'm pretty healthy, and I'm on and on it goes, and that breaks it right there.
I always have some things I can feel grateful for.
Those are really helpful tools: unskillful states of mind abandoned.
I want to make clear the business of abandoning unskillful states of mind does not mean avoiding real problems in your life.
It does not mean that I've always been very grateful to Zen over and over and over again, emphasizing you turn towards whatever is happening in your life, no matter how difficult you face it.
So if you have money problems, it's skillful to admit that, to look at the details, to feel what it feels like to have money problems, and then to go to, "What am I going to do about it?
Can I cut expenses?
Can I add some work so I make more money?"
Same thing if you have a health problem, same thing if you're grieving a loss or a death.
You have to feel the pain, acknowledge it in order to get through it.
Abandoning unskillful thinking has to do with abandoning thoughts like, "This is hopeless," "There's nothing I can do," "I'm so stupid," "How did this happen?"
The kind of repetitive critical thinking that so many of us can do.
And that's what the Buddha meant by abandoning unskillful thinking.

The first example happened at a board meeting a couple of months ago.
The board meets once a month, and at the very beginning of the year we set our meetings for the whole year so we don't have to figure out every month when we're going to meet again.
